Regarding the exposition of this treatise, it is analyzed through four gates: first, the causes for the arising of the treatise; second, the clarification of similarities and differences;

third, the determination of its ultimate purpose; and fourth, the explanation of the main text. Within the first gate, the causes for the arising of the treatise, it is further divided into: [The text continues with the specific sub-sections.]
Fourth:
first, clarifying the location of the division;
second, clarifying the year of the division.
The first part concerns the origins of the Three Clarities (*trividyā*).
The fourth part concerns the causes for composing this treatise, its author, and the fact that the Tathāgata taught that the essence of the Dharma is the single True Suchness (*tathatā*),
which is equal in benefiting sentient beings and without any distinction.
However, as the realization and understanding differ according to the capacities of the faculties,
there are distinctions between the gradual and the sudden, and thus differences in the teachings expounded.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
Although they are born from the same earth and moistened by the same rain,
the various plants and trees grow and develop differently.
As stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, it is like three animals crossing the same river and obtaining different depths.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* is like a precious jewel that rains down various things according to one's requests;
the *Anantamukhanirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* constantly speaks of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*),
yet through different modes of awakening and understanding, one attains various fruits.
Therefore, the Tathāgata’s teachings were spoken differently according to the capacities of his listeners.
Initially, for the sake of those such as the non-Buddhists,
he taught that the self does not exist and that phenomena do exist.
Next, in contrast to the Hīnayāna,
he refutes their attachment to the existence of dharmas and their claim that the teaching of dharmas is non-existent;
subsequently, he leads them toward reality and then reveals the teaching that [reality] is neither empty nor existent.
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* states:
"Since beginningless time, all classes of sentient beings have been ignorant of and have held perverse attachments regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
Arising from delusion and inciting karma, beings transmigrate through the five destinies.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he teaches the subtle principle of the Middle Way according to what is appropriate,
enabling all sentient beings to realize that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent.
Dwelling in the Middle Way, far removed from the origins of doubt and attachment, one should, according to what is appropriate, eliminate obstacles and cultivate each practice to fulfillment.
Thus, one attains *sambodhi* and realizes the bliss of *nirvāṇa*. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa...
And Vāśpa; although the Tripiṭaka was compiled in two separate locations,
the Buddha-dharma remained of one flavor for one hundred years.
At that time, there was the son of a shipowner named Mahādeva—according to Paramārtha’s *Commentary on the Sectarian Tenets*, he was from the country of Ayodhyā;

according to Master Ci’en’s *Commentary on the Wheel of the Doctrines*, he was from Central India—who left the household life to study the Path and became thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka. This is determined by the *Commentary on the Sectarian Tenets*, the *Commentary on the Wheel of the Doctrines*, and other such works.
The explanation of these five matters differs slightly from that found in Master Cien’s *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*.
This should be understood as the distinct explanations given for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna respectively;

this is fully detailed in those three locations as they are set forth there. Outside of the hundred years [after the Buddha’s passing], within the Kukkuṭārāma Monastery in the city of Pāṭaliputra—regarding which city, one should refer to the accounts in the *Great Tang Records on the Western Regions* and Paramārtha’s *Commentary on the Sectarian Tenets*—on the fifteenth day of the night, [he] spoke [this].
Mahādeva recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Having finished reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra, he then spoke five verses on the matters [of transgression], saying:
"Those who are led astray by others, those who are ignorant..."
Inducing others to enter through hesitation,
arising by means of sound—
this is called the true Buddha-teaching.
The elder sages all refused to grant this;
they immediately inverted that fourth statement and said:
"Your claim that this is not the Buddha's teaching is the reason the Śrāvaka vehicle split into two branches."
The assembly of noble ones,
at the time of the fundamental council,
took Mahākāśyapa as their teacher and thus became known as the Sthavira school.
Mahādeva and his followers took Vāsava as their teacher;
thus they are called the Mahāsāṃghika school.
Within two hundred years thereafter,
the Mahāsāṃghika school further split into nine;
this occurred within three hundred years.
The Sthavira school is divided into eleven branches, as fully explained in the *Saṃayabhedoparacanacakra* (Treatise on the Differentiation of the Sects) and the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā*.

The reasons for these divisions are each explained in detail in the *Śāstra on the Tenets of the Schools* by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. Formerly, when Ānanda was about to enter nirvāṇa, he thought to himself:
The Buddha prophesied that in the land of Kaśmīra—
now called Kāśmīra— there would be a bhikṣu named Madhyāntika who would reside in that country.
Having propagated the Eye of the Dharma,
he then entrusted the Dharma to the Venerable Madhyāntika,
desiring to establish a monastery in this country to propagate the Dharma.
In this country there is a mountain whose four sides are steep and precipitous while its center is extremely vast, with only a single gate.
A dragon king dwells within it, filling it with water.
The Venerable One, possessing supernatural powers, descended from the sky.
He addressed the Dragon King, saying,
"I beg for as much ground as a single sitting mat.
The Dragon King granted him this.
He then used his supernormal powers to cause his sitting mat to expand until it nearly reached the edge of the water.
He then requested from the Dragon King that fifteen li of surrounding water be left for the dragon to dwell in.
Consequently, he established a monastery; the monks became numerous, and the attendants (*karmadāna*) likewise grew many.
Later, as the monks gradually diminished while the slaves gradually formed a powerful group, they established themselves as kings.
For this reason, it was called the Kingdom of Nuo.
Later, the king of this country was named Kāśyapila;
he was exceedingly devout and faithful.
Whenever he invited his disciples into the palace to preach the Dharma,
various schools resided together there; consequently,
the teachings he delivered on different occasions varied from one another.
The king asked for the reason,
and [the minister] explained the circumstances in detail.
The king said, "Whose division shall we take now?"
At that time, Kātyāyanīputra, relying on the Sarvāstivāda school, composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* and presented it to the king.
The king approved of its broad dissemination; this account is transmitted above, though the original text has not been seen.
According to the tradition of Vasubandhu,
three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was an arhat named Kātyāyanīputra.
Mātṛceṭa was named after his mother;
he had previously gone forth as a monk in the Sarvāstivāda school.
He was originally a native of Central India.
Later, he went to the kingdom of Kaśmīra,
which is located in Western India.
Together with five hundred arhats and five hundred bodhisattvas,
they compiled the Abhidharma of the Sarvāstivāda school and kept it secret so that it did not circulate;
for a long time, it was not seen in the Five Regions of India.
Later, in the kingdom of Ayodhyā in Eastern India,
there was a Dharma master named Vasubhadra,
who was brilliant and possessed great wisdom.
He went there to study and mastered the recitation of the *Lokottaravāda* scriptures,
as described in detail therein.
Later, Kumāralāta and Śrīlāta both extensively composed treatises.

At the beginning of the Hongchu era, there were teachings that caused sentient beings to cling to existence, and the teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma had for the most part disappeared. More than two hundred years later, the Bodhisattvas Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva both appeared in the world from South India.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra as a commentary on the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā,
and he also composed the Akutobhayā-śāstra,
totaling one hundred thousand stanzas.
The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Middle Treatise) emerged from the Akṣayamati school and consists of five hundred verses;
there are also works such as the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* (Twelve Gate Treatise).
Nāgārjuna’s disciple, the Bodhisattva Āryadeva, composed the *Śata-śāstra* (Hundred Verse Treatise) and other works.
This is explained in detail in the *Dharmatrāta-dharmaguptaka-śāstra* (The Tradition of the Transmission of the Dharma) and the legends concerning Nāgārjuna and others.
It was taught as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in order to refute the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena held by the followers of the Hīnayāna and various non-Buddhist schools.
At that time, many were attached to emptiness. Nine hundred years later, in the region of North India known as Puruṣapura—
this being translated as "Country of Men"—
there was a state preceptor who was a brāhmaṇa.
His clan name was Kauśika.
He had three sons, all named Vasubandhu,
which in Chinese is translated as Tianqin (Heavenly Relative).
Now, he is called Vasubandhu, which in this language means "World-Kinsman" (Shiqin).
Although they share the same name, a distinct title has been established for him.
On the third day, his mother entered the order in the Sarvāstivāda school and attained the fruit of arhatship;
she was also known by the name Pilindavatsa,
"Pilindi" being her mother's name.
"Baba" is translated as "son" or "child.
His eldest brother possessed the spiritual capacity (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva and also went forth into the religious life within the Sarvāstivāda school.
Later, having become free from desire, he contemplated the meaning of emptiness;
unable to attain entry [into that state], he attempted to take his own life.
At that time, there was the Arhat Piṇḍola.
While in Pūrvavideha he observed this matter;
coming from that region, he spoke of the meaning of the Śrāvaka-vehicle’s contemplation of emptiness, yet his mind remained unsettled, thinking that such a principle could not be correct.
Therefore, he ascended to Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya Bodhisattva,
who expounded for him the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness.
Upon returning, he engaged in contemplation and immediately attained awakening;
consequently, he was named Asaṅga,
which in this [language] means "The Unattached."
Thereafter, he went several times to the Tuṣita Heaven to inquire about the meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras from Maitreya; however,
when he explained them to others, most did not believe what they heard.
He immediately made a vow,
requesting that Maitreya Bodhisattva descend to preach the Mahāyāna,
so that all sentient beings who see him might gain faith and acceptance.
Then, in accordance with his wish, at the time of nightfall,
he emitted a great radiance and gathered the assembly of those with karmic connection;
in the kingdom of Yūṣa, he expounded the *Saptadaśabhūmi-śāstra*.
As each passage was recited, its meaning was explained accordingly.
After four months and seventeen nights, the treatises were completed;
although they were all in the same hall, only Asanga was able to draw near to Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Others could only hear from afar,
or some perceived it differently;
at that time, Master Asanga explained it further for their sake.
Consequently, other people only then began to believe in and accept the teachings of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The second son also left the household life within the Sarvāstivāda school;
he was profoundly learned and widely erudite, thoroughly mastering all the classical scriptures.
His divine talent was brilliant and peerless;
his observance of the precepts was pure and lofty, beyond compare.
Since the brothers possessed distinct names, [they were known by their respective appellations].
Therefore, the Dharma Master is simply called Vasubandhu.
The remaining details of his life and circumstances are as extensively described in his original biography.
Based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, he composed numerous treatises.
The explanation that the propagation of the Mahāyāna is neither empty nor existent,
as well as the composition of this treatise,
the combined and edited translations of the ten masters' commentaries, are all consistent with the *Shuyao*.
However, it was only one thousand and one hundred years later that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla appeared in the world,
composing this commentary (*Vādanyāya*) as well as the *Śataka-vṛtti*.
The Bodhisattva Bhāviveka also appeared at the same time and composed the *Tarkajvālā* (The Blaze of Reasoning).
At this time, the Mahāyāna is precisely debating emptiness and existence.
Thus far, the meanings of the four gates have been explained in general;
may the wise understand them.
This constitutes the origin of this treatise.
Second, regarding the clarification of similarities and differences,
it is further divided into four parts.
First, there is a distinction in the benefits of the teachings;
second, there are differences in the timing and the capacities of those benefited;
third, the doctrines expressed differ from one another.
Fourth, their essential natures differ, as explained in detail in the *Fayuan zhulin* (Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma). Question:

Regarding the two principles previously mentioned—benefit through the wheel (*cakrabhoga*) and benefit through meaning (*arthabhoga*)—how do they differ? Answer: "Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the designation based on the principle that is expressed (*lakṣya*).
The term "wheel" (*cakra*) refers to the path of severance.
These two meanings each pertain to a single approach;

hence it is said that the wheel has two meanings and two benefits. Question: When the teaching is matched against the capacities of sentient beings, there are distinctions among the three periods of the teaching.

It is not yet clear whether the substance (*tattva*) of the wheel is distinct or identical. Answer: Since the faculties and natures (*indriya-gotra*) differ, the substances of the wheels are distinct.
According to the initial teachings of the *sāśravābhidharma*, the substance is as previously explained;
however, within the *anāśrava* (emptiness) teachings, the substance differs slightly.
It takes the eightfold noble path of emptiness as its essence;
it takes the wisdom that realizes the principle of emptiness as its essence;
and it takes the teaching that explains emptiness as its cause.
Taking the preparatory knowledge that realizes emptiness as its cause,
taking emptiness as its object of focus,
and taking the remaining factors of enlightenment and so forth as its companions.
Taking the emptiness of the path, concentration, and precepts as its retinue,
and taking the emptiness of bodhi and nirvāṇa as its fruit—
if this is the essence of the wheel of Dharma at the third stage.
Combining the previous two [positions] also results in what is not correct.

What is correct is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the fourth fascicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-vyākhyā*. Question: What benefit is there in explaining these secret words? Answer: According to the eighth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are ten fruits.
That is to say, it is for the sake of enabling the speaker of the Dharma to easily establish and summarize the meaning;
furthermore, so that one may enter the ranks of the wise through the determination of arguments in debate.
For these ten benefits, he speaks words of mystery. Regarding the benefit of inquiry, there are both those that are clear and those that are obscure.

The elucidation of principle has both exoteric and esoteric aspects;
within these meanings, there are those that are fully understood and those that are not.
For all, according to their capacities, these serve to extinguish hindrances.
"All wheels [of dharma] are indeed wheels. Furthermore, the *Yaoji xu* (Preface to the Essential Collection) explains the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, stating:
"As for those who claim that the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) was spoken by the compilers and is not the actual word of the Buddha—this is not so; it was spoken by Bhāviveka and others."
That is not a skillful interpretation.

One should say that the words of Bhāviveka and others are intended for the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and are considered definitive (nītārtha) in that context, without intending them to refer to the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If one were to claim that something is not the word of the Buddha simply because it appears contradictory,
it would render the entire holy teaching untrustworthy. Regarding the fourfold classification of the Dharma Garden into definitive (*nītārtha*) and non-definitive (*neyārtha*) meanings,
the *Jiyaoji* (Essential Compendium) states:
Furthermore, there is one gate:
to be attached to names is called "not understanding," while not being attached to names is "understanding."
Therefore, the *Īśvararāja-bodhisattva-sūtra*, in its first fascicle, states:
"As for sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), all sūtras are of definitive meaning,
because they rely upon the meaning."
Because all phenomena are inexpressible,
a bodhisattva is said to have thus realized the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
If a person, regarding all sutras...
That which cannot be understood in this way according to its meaning is called "of incomplete meaning" (neyārtha).
Why is it called "of incomplete meaning"?
Because such a person does not understand the meaning.
According to this scriptural passage, it says:
"This person does not understand the meaning; therefore, it is called 'of non-definitive meaning' (neyārtha).
It does not mean that the scripture itself is judged to be of non-definitive meaning.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"O Sovereign King Bodhisattva, for one who relies on such a meaning and pursues the Dharma,
all sutras are of definitive meaning."
If one does not rely on this,
then all sūtras are of provisional meaning (neyārtha).
According to this principle:
One must not cling to the notion that all sūtras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
if one clings [to such a view], then all sūtras would be of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
It cannot be argued that this is due to the person themselves being unable to understand.
He then judged that the holy teachings were also not definitive.
The *Yāojíejì* (Essential Collection of Explanations) states:
"That which can cause either faults or merits to arise."
"It is not so. This [term] applies universally to all Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras; this judgment, however, is not thus.
If it were the case that a fault arises simply because one does not understand, then it would be called "not understanding."
It would also have to be called unwholesome and it would also have to be called with-outflows; thus,
it would not be a designation that accords with reality.
Because there are many errors,
the correct explanation should now be stated as follows:
according to the Dharma, it is divided into four parts.
As clarified in the *Fayuan*,
one further adds the criterion of the person [who taught it]:
that which is understood through direct confrontation and is free from attachment is designated as "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).
For those who cling [to them], these are called *neyārtha* (of provisional meaning).

Regarding the two truths, as explained in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*: Question: Why did the Tathāgata first teach the doctrine of existence (*astitva*) and later discuss the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?
Question: Does this subsequently expound the teaching that is neither empty nor existent? Answer:
Based on those of indeterminate lineage who have not yet set out [on the path], it is intended merely to cause them to feel shame and realize that the self they cling to does not exist.
There are only the phenomena of the aggregates, bases,
and elements which are called "instruction";
they are for those who have already set out and attained small fruits.

It causes them to proceed toward the Great [Vehicle] and subsequently realize the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena; observing that the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields they grasp at do not exist is called the teaching of emptiness.
Subsequently, for those who set out upon any of the vehicles, [it serves as a foundation].
This reveals that what is grasped is non-existent;
it is not that the grasping itself exists,
nor is it an absolute emptiness.
Nor is it the case that all [teachings] are so; rather, they constitute teachings that are neither empty nor existent.
These teachings are expounded in three stages for the sake of those who possess a sense of shame and awakening.
If one considers sudden enlightenment, there is no distinction between three periods.
Furthermore, the teachings spoken were not necessarily fixed in such a sequence of three periods;
rather, they were all categorized according to the similarity of the categories of meaning they express.
It is expected that those of indeterminate lineage would be in the third period;
otherwise, the *Avataṃsaka* was taught by the World-Honored One during the second seven-day interval,
which could instead be placed after the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras for those who might attain realization through a sense of shame.
Only now does the exposition begin, which is categorized as the third [section]. This has two meanings:
first, in terms of chronological sequence;
second, in terms of thematic categories.
In terms of the preceding and succeeding sections, there are also two meanings:
first, the emptiness of persons is taught;
second, the emptiness of phenomena is taught.
Second, first there is the teaching of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which implicitly indicates the existence of phenomena (*dharma-sattva*);
next, there is the teaching of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which implicitly indicates the non-existence of phenomena;
and finally, it clearly reveals that the objects apprehended by the two types of grasping—toward persons and phenomena—do not exist.
If one is free from the two attachments, the ultimate and the conventional are not non-existent.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"The conditioned and the unconditioned are called 'existence'."
"I and what belongs to me are taught to be empty. Question: If these various teachings are based on entering [the path] gradually, they constitute the third period.
The teachings of the third period are intended universally for those who have set out upon all vehicles.
To which vehicle does this present treatise primarily apply?
If it is for the sake of the three vehicles, how does it refute them?
If it applies only to the Mahāyāna and not to the third [vehicle], what then? Answer: The passages refuting the self are applicable to all three vehicles.
It subverts the positions of the two vehicles so that they may enter only the Great Vehicle;
furthermore, it subverts their attachments but does not subvert those vehicles themselves.

Therefore, it is generally categorized as threefold. If this is so, since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also speaks of "subverting the vehicles," it should belong to the second period. Answer: It is taught as one in terms of principle, in contrast to those of indeterminate lineage.
By refuting the attachment to the distinctness of principles, one causes them to incline toward the Mahāyāna.
If their fixed lineage and contemplative practices differ, it is explained as being like medicinal herbs;
because there are distinctions among the vehicles, [the teaching] can be universally applied.
However, this sutra was taught primarily because [the previous teachings] were largely indeterminate;

it specifically teaches that the One Vehicle is the task to be accomplished by all śrāvakas and others. If that is so, then since the third period was intended for everyone universally, [how can there be further distinctions?]
Why is it that the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states, "I do not reveal this to the foolish and ordinary," while the *Abhidharma* states, "I reveal this to the Victors"?
Answer: It is said that for the most part, during the three periods [of teaching], [the Buddha] taught it to all.
It is not said that each individual syllable constitutes the three vehicles respectively.
Rather, within the various passages of this treatise, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, it is applicable to all three [vehicles] throughout;
therefore, there is no contradiction. Question: Since the teaching was explained in three periods specifically for those of gradual enlightenment...
That is to say, the third period was also taught for those who gradually awaken and aspire toward the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

If it was intended solely for those of the Great Vehicle, how can it be said that it was taught universally for all? Answer: Because their faculties were matured and their wisdom had already attained penetration, it was taught for them.
To clarify that the emptiness observed by those of the three vehicles is the same, it is said that all phenomena are "everything.
Although within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* there are instances where each of the three vehicles attains their respective benefits, [the ultimate nature remains one].

Because it has not yet clearly explained that dharmas are neither empty nor existent, it belongs to the second category. If one were to establish [the teaching] as "simultaneous" (*ekakāla*) based on sudden enlightenment, how would this differ from the ancients? The *Fayuan* does not permit this. Answer: The ancients established "one time" (*ekakāla*). However, their meaning differs from ours. They maintained that the Buddha’s preaching was simultaneous because his wisdom and compassion were both constant; thus, they designated it as "one time. Our position is that although the Buddha’s wisdom and compassion are indeed constant, the capacities of sentient beings are not. Therefore, we do not establish it as "one time" based on the constancy of the Buddha’s wisdom and compassion. Rather, we establish it as "one time" based on the fact that the teaching is simultaneously heard by those of sharp faculties who have already attained realization. This is why it is distinct from the ancients. Furthermore, the ancients established "one time" based on the principle that the Dharma is non-dual and that there is no distinction between the beginning and the end. We, however, establish "one time" based on the principle that the teaching is received all at once by those of sharp faculties. Thus, the two are not the same. Moreover, the ancients established "one time" based on the principle that the Buddha’s body is eternally abiding. We, however, establish "one time" based on the principle that the teaching is received all at once by those of sharp faculties. Thus, the two are not the same. Furthermore, the ancients established "one time" based on the principle that the Buddha’s preaching is uninterrupted. We, however, establish "one time" based on the principle that the teaching is received all at once by those of sharp faculties. Thus, the two are not the same. Finally, the ancients established "one time" based on the principle that the Buddha’s teaching is equal for all. We, however, establish "one time" based on the principle that the teaching is received all at once by those of sharp faculties. Thus, the two are not the same. It is for these reasons that our establishment of "one time" differs from that of the ancients. This is what is meant by "one time. If one were to establish "one time" based on the principle that the teaching is received all at once by those of sharp faculties, then even the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas could be called "one time," for they too are taught all at once to those of sharp faculties. However, this is not so. Why? Because the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not the ultimate vehicle. Only the Mahāyāna is the ultimate vehicle. Therefore, we establish "one time" solely based on the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the ancients established "one time" based on the principle that the Buddha’s teaching is without beginning or end. Some say it is called "sudden" (*sa-er*) because one encounters a new object;
others explain that it is called "sudden" because it is not preceded by deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*).
What constitutes the correct [position]?
The explanation states that the treatise maintains [the view] that it arises spontaneously (*svarasataḥ*).
If one says it refers to a new object, no textual evidence for this is seen.
However, according to the principles of reasoning, there ought to be two meanings.
Now, I say this is not so.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third [section], states:
Furthermore, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) spontaneously becomes distracted and takes as its object a realm with which it is not familiar,
the arising of desire and so forth is termed "sudden" (*ābhoga*).
Since it is said that taking an unfamiliar realm as an object refers to a new object, [the desire] arises immediately upon encountering it.
If that which is merely spontaneous distraction toward an object, not accompanied by desire, is called "sudden" (*ābhoga*),
then except for the sixth consciousness,
at all other times there would be nothing but the "sudden" state, and no other mental states would exist.
In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), all [cognitions] are exclusively instances of spontaneous, distracted engagement with objects.

There are further similarities and differences, which I shall not describe in detail for fear of prolixity. As for what is called "manifestation through aggregation," it is as when one says, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*).
There is an explanation which says:
In the West, there are three interpretations.
The first states that when various syllables are uttered, they are immediately perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In seeking the preceding object, one does not take names and so forth as conditions, but merely apprehends the characteristic of sound;
upon reaching the mind of determination, the three characteristics—
namely, sound, name, and syllable— are fully manifested.
When "practice" (行) is spoken, six appear;
when "non-existence" (無) is spoken, nine appear;
when the character for "permanence" (常) is spoken, twelve signs appear.
Together with the phrases, there are fourteen dharmas that are explained;
these are fully assembled only after sixteen moments of mind.
That is to say, within each of the four characters, there are four moments of mind respectively.
This refers to the four types of sudden engagement (*sahaja*) for each of the ear and the mind,
as well as the four types of seeking (*paryeṣaka*) and determining (*niścaya*) for the mind respectively.
One opinion holds that seeking is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, because they take names and so forth as their objects,
the four types of seeking minds also obtain a collection [of objects] in their respective order.
One attains three, six, nine, and fourteen [minds].
One should understand, according to the preceding [analysis], that twelve minds are fully assembled.
One school says: "The ear-consciousness takes the same object as the mental consciousness, and the mental consciousness also takes names (*nāman*) and so forth as its objects."
Regarding this, there are two explanations.
One says that each of the four types of sudden-cognition minds (*saterīna-citta*) obtains only three [objects];
because they do not take the past as an object and are attained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), their accumulation is not mentioned.
It is only when the mind seeks [the object] that it is designated as the essence of the teaching (*deśanā*).
One view holds that because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) simultaneous with the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) may not be manifest, it is able to take the past as its object.
That is to say, within the eight moments of mind, [the factors] are fully assembled;
yet now it is said that there are still omissions.
Furthermore, in the first explanation, the moments of mind traversed are many while the dharmas assembled are few.
What is it that is accumulated upon the mental consciousness? For what reason does the sūtra speak of four "sudden" moments of ear-consciousness?
Could it be that you admit the mental consciousness does not apprehend the primary object (svabhāva), but instead takes as its object only the sound transformed by the ear-consciousness?

Since it is already granted that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) arise simultaneously and each directly perceives its own objective essence (*svabhāva*),
then while twelve moments of mind may manifest through the mental consciousness,
sixteen should not.
If one were to take "ear" in its most superficial sense,
it should be understood as the ear taking sound as its object;
in that case, there would necessarily be eighteen dharmas.

If one were to speak of only fourteen factors based on the similarity of their sound, then one should likewise speak of only twelve minds based on the similarity of the mind; however, according to the actual teaching, the four sudden occurrences involving the ear are excluded.
However, it is only through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that the twelve types of mind manifest.
As for the phenomena accumulated therein: there are four moments of sound, four syllables, four names, and the four referents denoted by those names.
That is, the four intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, there is one phrase together with the specific meaning expressed by that phrase;
these eighteen factors, when combined, manifest as a collection.
This is based on a single characteristic;
however, if within a single syllable and so forth there appear immeasurable syllables and so forth,
the principle is not fixed.

Regarding the explanation of the various consciousnesses within the five minds and the three natures, the determination of their correctness or error will be clarified below in the fifth section. Furthermore, concerning the "constant" aspect among the two aspects previously discussed regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one must decisively understand that while all designations are subject to flux and flow, there is no such permanence therein.
There is an interpretation that all four characters possess a definitive meaning.
The *Yaoji* states: "If this interpretation were absent, there would be a deficiency in principle;
although other interpretations exist, they still do not exhaust the full meaning."
That is to say, when a proponent wishes to establish impermanence, they formulate a syllogism (pramāṇa) against an opponent, stating: "All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent.
Although the opponent hears the first three [members] of this formulation, [they may still harbor doubts].
However, no certain understanding has yet arisen regarding what is being established;
it is only when the syllable *nitya* (eternal) is uttered that such a certain understanding arises.
Therefore, the first three syllables have not yet reached a state of certainty.
It continues:
"If one follows this interpretation,
it is only after establishing the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that certainty arises."
This thesis is established according to this same principle and intent.
One should reflect upon this point:
if there is no certainty while [the reason] has not yet been understood, then certainty arises only after the statement of the reason and the example.
Furthermore, regarding Ximing’s interpretation that all four characters are definitive:
if one has not yet heard what the various characters refer to,
and since one does not yet know which phenomena those various [characters] refer to, how can they be determined?
How could there be certainty?
If one says that there is a certain mind that knows these various sounds with certainty,
then when pronouncing the syllable "saṃ," there should be three certainties.
One definitively knows that formations are designated by various terms, and one definitively knows that these various terms refer to formations;
for if one did not definitively know that various terms refer to formations, understanding would not arise.
The other two [categories] are to be understood accordingly.
One should immediately synthesize this with the six determinations (*ṣaḍ-vidha-niścaya*).

It is not appropriate for there to be only four, as that would result in the fault of either addition or subtraction. Furthermore, what is stated in the *Yāo jí* (Essential Compendium) does not fully accord with reason.
While one may establish formal inference (*pramāṇa*) against an opponent as described, if one merely expounds the Dharma without establishing formal inference, the determinations may be absent.
Therefore, the *Fayuan* (Garden of Dharma) generally explains the teachings by way of intention.
Having definitively understood what those various terms refer to, one gives rise to a mind of certainty;
it is said that there are seven minds, or twelve, and so forth.
Therefore, there is no fault.
One should not judge the extent [of the teachings] solely based on the meaning and intent of what was spoken upon awakening.
Since other points were repeated, why would they not have been stated in full? The *Yaoji* says:
The *Fayuan* states that one should not commit any evil; this is based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
[It concerns] syllables (*vyañjana*), word-bodies (*pada-kāya*), multi-syllable bodies, names (*nāman*), name-bodies (*nāma-kāya*), and multi-name bodies (*nāma-kāya*), and so forth.
To claim that when one hears a single phrase there are fifty-one dharmas present—
meaning that within the understanding arising from hearing the meaning of a single phrase of a sutra,
such a multitude of dharmas must necessarily manifest before one— does not correctly grasp the intent of the *Dharmāyana*.
Furthermore, according to the method of a single phrase, it is as follows:
for example, when five syllables are spoken, there may be one name, which is a "name" (nāman); such name-bodies (nāmakāya) include fifteen types and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "the manifestation of the fifty-one [mental factors] is not fixed":

when one hears a single word, there may be an allowance for their simultaneous aggregation, as in the case of the method described among the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-niyata*) in the fifth fascicle. The *Yāo jí* (Essential Compendium) states:
For this reason, there are syllables that are not subsumed under names.
A single syllable does not constitute a phrase;
because syllables serve as the basis for both [names and phrases], eighteen dharmas exist therein.
That is to say, there are fifteen syllables (vyañjana),
five phonemes (akṣara),
and four syllable-bodies (vyañjanakāya).
The six multi-syllabic bases (*bahuvyañjana-kāya*) are to be understood according to the established method. This is not the case here;
rather, one should state that there are fifteen [bases], including the single syllables (*vyañjana*), the multi-syllabic bases, and so forth.
The following should be understood accordingly:
whereas a single phrase, a single name, and a single referent meaning [function as a unit],
this is not the case here.
It is universally taught in all [treatises] that names are established based on syllables and phrases are established based on names.
How could it be that what is not a name is not to be so designated?
If it were otherwise, then even terms such as "suffering" (duḥkha) and "emptiness" (śūnyatā) would likewise not be subsumed under the category of names.
Furthermore, since [the Buddha] himself later judged that both names for the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are correct,
why is it that in this instance there is only one name?
Moreover, one should not say that there is only a single referent.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises,
there are two types of establishment:
first, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, regarding differentiation:
names express intrinsic nature,
while phrases express differentiation.
Are the intrinsic nature and its differentiation not two distinct meanings?
Or do you say they are one meaning?
Furthermore, it says:
If one does not establish the method according to the characteristics of consciousness and by analogy with its meaning,
it would not be merely fifty and seventy-one dharmas combined;
there would be fifteen syllables.
There are thirty-five names,
twenty phrases,
and the meanings they express.
This intention may consist of a phrase formed by two names,
three names, or four names.
Fifth, because they constitute a phrase.
Thirty-five names consist of twenty phrases;
thus, the meaning of a single character constitutes five names.
The second type, the phrase consisting of two names, has four [instances],
with two combined as each. The third type,
the phrase consisting of three names, has three [instances].
Three and three combine;
the fourth is called the "perfected phrase" (vākya) and has two [parts].
Four and four combine.
The fifth, "establishing phrases," has one [category];
when five are combined and explained, there are ten phrases. As for the second, "establishing names," since there are four within the category of names...
The second type, phrases consisting of two words, has three varieties;
the third type, phrases consisting of three words, has two varieties;
and the fourth type, phrases consisting of four words, has one variety.
Furthermore, there are six types of phrases: two phrases consisting of three characters each, one phrase consisting of three names, and one phrase consisting of four characters.
Among these, two types consist of names forming a phrase, while one consists of names forming a phrase and one consists of characters forming a phrase.
There is one phrase, totaling twenty phrases.
Five characters form a name; since the name is singular, there is not a single name that lacks a phrase.
And including one [instance of] expressing meaning, there are seventy-one in total. This is also not the case.
Why? If we discuss syllables, there are five.
There are fifteen types of names.
There are five types of names formed from a single syllable,
and four types of names formed from two syllables.
There are three names consisting of three syllables,
two names consisting of four syllables,
and one name consisting of five syllables.
If the body of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*) and the body of names (*nāma-kāya*) are combined with those [previously mentioned],
there are no further distinct names or syllables;
together with the phrases, these twenty and thirty-five constitute the meanings to be expressed.
The syllable *pada* consists of fifteen *vyañjana-kāyas*.
The name (*nāman*) consists of thirty-five; the phrase (*pada*) consists of twenty.
Altogether, there are one hundred and five.
If one were to further include the phrases (*pada*), the phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), and their underlying sounds (*śabda*), these would be even more numerous.
Thus, for now, we speak only of seventy-one [factors], as there would otherwise be the fault of over- or under-counting.
This is merely a rough presentation according to the *Dharmayuan* (Fa-yuan), intended to clarify the nature of the expressive [factors].

Furthermore, since this detailed discussion is not exhaustive, there is an error. Question: On what basis can it be known that words establish names, and names establish phrases? Answer: The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, chapter five, states:
Regarding the collection of all names, the *Śata-śāstra*, chapter eight,
states: "However, in the world, according to the transformations of their own minds,
people claim that various syllables combine to form a name."
Furthermore, it is said that the combination of multiple names constitutes a phrase;
thus, one knows that such [a definition] follows. Regarding the subsequent account of his own explanation, there are twelve sections in total, comprising both the fundamental and the derivative.
To the original four gates, two more are added; that is,
the latter four gates take up the signless and dependent origination, which,
together with the former, constitute six.
Seventh, the establishment of the three natures as their essence:
this relies upon the four realities of the *Vyākhyāyukti* and other texts— namely, the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected—
and further relies upon the four realities of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*.
Ninth, it relies on the five characteristics,
namely the expressive characteristics such as yoga and the expressed characteristics, and so forth.
Tenth, it relies on the five dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four differences regarding these characteristics, names, and so forth:
first, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
second, the *Madhyānta-vibhāga-śāstra*.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in three fascicles and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* both clarify the reasons for this as explained in the eighth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Eleventh, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81, it says:
"The essence of the sūtra is twofold:
first, the expressive text."
Second, the meaning expressed.
Within both the words and the meaning, there are many dharmas that together constitute the essence of the sūtra.
Regarding these twelve [categories], they are subsumed within the hundred dharmas.
Since the three categories and five dharmas are common to the three vehicles,
those that are minor or mixed are not mentioned;
only those pertaining to the Mahāyāna are taken up.
Furthermore, in brief, there are two [categories].
First, regarding the general presentation of their essential nature, there are four:
suchness (*tathatā*), consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), signlessness (*animitta*), and causal conditions (*pratyaya*).
There are eight distinct [categories],
because they share a common essential nature and yet are distinct individual phenomena.
I shall briefly state the general meaning;
I will not describe it in detail for fear of prolixity.
Regarding those who take the Three Refuges:
It is further divided into four parts:
first, the Guizang;
second, the Guifen.
The three refuges and the vehicles are both as explained in the "Chapter on the Divisions and Vehicles" of the *Fayuan zhulin*.
Regarding the names of the four refuges:
First, the analysis;
second, the return.
There are three parts to the analysis.
First, distinguishing the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaṭ-samāsa*).

This is also as explained in the *Fayuan* (Garden of Dharma), where the general and specific designations are briefly examined and their divergent origins are distinguished. Furthermore, regarding the six types of analysis, there is an explanation that distinguishes them into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) based on the *taddhitārtha* (dependent) and *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds.
There are cases where the *bhartṛpada* (possessive compound) is not the primary basis,
such as "the aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*),
because "clinging" (*upādāna*) is the object [of clinging] and not the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*).
There are cases where the dependent (upādāya) is the primary referent rather than the possessor (upādātr),
such as "the grasping of the aggregates" (skandhānām upādāna).
This [case you cite] should not be so.
If the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) and *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds were not mutually inclusive, there would have to be seven types of interpretation.
Some explain that the six types of interpretation can be condensed into three categories:
first, those where the members are identical and not distinct; [the other two categories follow].
1. The function-based compound (*karmadhāraya*) and the numeral-based compound (*dvigu*).
2. Distinct entities that are not identical, which are contradictory yet proximate.
3. Those that are both identical and distinct.
Regarding the *adhīśvara-svāmin* (possessor) and *tad-utpatti* (that which possesses),
their principles may be confused when considered;
however, if the dharma being explained is pervasive, there is no obstruction.
According to the six types of etymological analysis (*ṣaḍ-vyākhyāna*), the actual nature [of the term] is not necessarily fixed.
For instance, in the case of the "four abandonments" (*catur-prahāṇa*), the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) refers to the mental factor of diligence (*vīrya*),
while the number "four" refers to their enumeration.
This is immediately inconsistent.
How could they be of the same substance?
Furthermore, it is like the contradiction between the five consciousness-bodies and the stage of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*).
These two dharmas are explained by combining them into one location while distinguishing their respective natures; for instance,
the *Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā Bhūmi* (the Ground Associated with the Five Consciousnesses) is itself that ground,
and it does not take the five consciousnesses associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as its ground.
Nor is it the case that the five [consciousnesses] are identical to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and so forth.

Since it is stated that they "correspond to the ground of the five groups of consciousness" (*pañcavijñānakāyasaṃprayuktā bhūmiḥ*), how could these be of a separate substance? The *Yaoji* (Essential Collection) says:
The Three Piṭakas have traditionally been categorized into four types:
first, using one's own [knowledge] rather than that of others;
second, using the knowledge of others rather than one's own.
Third, used by both self and others;
fourth, used by neither self nor others.
Regarding the function of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-karma*), there is only the first case.
The dependent (tatpuruṣa) compound is only the third [type];
the possessive (bahuvrīhi) is only the second;
and the contradictory (dvandva) is only the fourth.
The neighboring [factors] apply to two or three;
those accompanied by a number apply to the first and the third.
This continues up to the three phrases accompanied by a number, which correspond to the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); that is, the first phrase [of the four right efforts].
The fourth [set] is the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Just as the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) correspond to the third phrase,
the four [abandonments] belong to desire and so forth, and are therefore not bases of power.
As it is said, "the Dharma Master who is a Tripitaka master" constitutes the third case.
If one were to say merely "the Tripitaka," that would be the second case;
for while "three" refers to the three collections (*piṭaka*) and "pitaka" refers to the collection, neither term individually denotes a person.
That explanation by Śrīlāta is extremely extensive;
fearing it would be too cumbersome, I have not provided it in full.
However, based on this explanation, there are points of confusion and inconsistency.
One should reflect upon the six types of etymological explanation to eliminate confusion.
Second, the identification of the four names:
namely, teaching (śāsana), principle (yukti), practice (pratipatti), and fruit (phala).
Now, the Tripitaka Master Zhendi has five types of names: first, the name according to meaning;
second, the name according to characteristics.
Third, the skillful means;
fourth, the fruits;
fifth, ultimate purity.
That which is "utterly pure" refers to the purity of the *āgama* (scriptural transmission), and thus it is the teaching (*deśanā*).
However, there is no difference between the two broad categories of meaning (*artha*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because that which is expressed possesses the correct, actual principle, it is called the purity of meaning (*arthaviśuddhi*).

Because it is pure and free from the conceptual proliferations of increase and decrease, these are now combined to establish four names for the principle that is the object of expression (*vācya*). This section is divided into two parts;
first, the different ways in which the names are established.
Regarding the subsequent establishment of the name "manas" (mind), as for the differences in these designations:
first, according to the teachings, there are three names.
The first is "words devoid of meaning."
It is like the treatises on the four Vedas;
when Brahmins recite them, their voices possess superior, middling, and inferior qualities that are exceedingly pleasant to hear.
Yet, if one seeks the underlying principle by following the sound alone, there is no meaningful purpose whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called meaningless speech.
As the Vedic treatises state:
"I have already drunk the nectar."
Having attained non-death, I have entered the fire-light.
May the devas and kinsmen consider me as having churned the ocean of milk to produce the nectar of immortality.
If one drinks it, one attains immortality.
Although these words are recited with an excellent melody,
they are called "meaningless" because they possess no meaning whatsoever.
Second is false speech (*mithyāvāda*).

For example, the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) also speak of cause and effect, but because their explanations are deviant and perverse, it is called "false. Third is speech according to the truth (*yathārthavāda*), such as the explanation of the principles of cause and effect as taught in the Buddha-dharma.
Suffering and its origin constitute the causes and effects of the mundane world;
cessation and the path constitute the causes and effects of the supramundane.
Because it is called "Suchness" (tathatā) because it is true, it is termed "the meaning of Suchness. Furthermore, based on this principle, there are three names.
First, the meaning of superimposition (*samāropa*).
For example, as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) assert that contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are permanent, blissful, self, and pure;
therefore, it is called the meaning of superimposition.
Second is the meaning of deprecation (*apavāda*).

For example, as stated in the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), to falsely deny the existence of the causes and effects of wholesome and unwholesome actions is called the meaning of deprecation.
Third, the meaning of accordance with the essence (*tattvārtha-anuloma*).

As the Buddha has taught, that which exists is said to exist, and that which does not exist is said not to exist; because this accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called "accordance with the essence. There are also three names based on practice (*pratipatti*).
First, causes that conform to worldly conventions,
such as serving one's sovereign with total loyalty or maintaining faithfulness toward friends according to secular treatises.
Second, causes that are deviant and perverse.
This refers to the false precepts and so forth falsely imagined by the various non-Buddhists.

Regarding the "cause within the three bases," this refers to practicing the Middle Way according to the Buddha’s teaching, thereby remaining free from the extremes of suffering and pleasure. Regarding the "three names based on the fruit":
First, the fruit of flattery and deception:
such as when a minister follows the sovereign’s command to obtain undeserved honor and the like.
Second, the fruit of falsehood:
This refers to how various non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize states such as the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as being nirvāṇa and so forth.
Third are the supramundane fruits.
Regarding the names established for the bodhi and nirvāṇa attained by the three vehicles as taught by the Buddha:
these four names are established in order to attain the four purities.
The term "in accordance with reality" (yathārtha) is established in order to attain the purity of the teaching.
Teachings that are unadulterated and do not exceed the meaning as it truly is can be established so as to be indestructible and capable of leading to the realization of truth.
Teachings that express what is incorrect are easily destroyed.

Because one cannot realize the principle [through mere words], the term "conforming to the meaning" (*yathārtha*) is established; because it serves as the basis for attaining the purity of realizing the principle, the name "conforming to the essence" (*tattvānugata*) is established.
When the principle possesses increase or decrease, the correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) cannot enter into that principle when it observes it.
When explained in accordance with the essence, the principle of observing through right knowledge is easy to enter.
Therefore, establishing the meaning of "conformity to the essence" is called the purity of practice; thus, the name "cause for abiding in the middle" is established.
Because the practice of the middle way is contrasted with both worldly conformity and deviant causes, those two can be turned away from,
whereas this practice of the middle way cannot be turned away from;
for in the practice of the middle way, one internally contemplates the elements (*dhātu*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).
The inclination toward deviance and the practice of deviance can be transformed;
however, when one contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, they cannot be transformed.
This is because the contemplative practices pertaining to the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths are applied in contrast to the contemplation of the aggregates and other such categories.
The aggregates and so forth can be transformed when viewed through the practice of the two emptinesses; the four truths can be transformed when viewed through the practice of the four truths.
The practice of the two emptinesses is irreversible;
since the wisdom of the two emptinesses is irreversible,
the wisdom that realizes truth is likewise irreversible.
Because it is irreversible,
this very true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) constitute the essence of correct practice;
they are able to cause the fruit obtained to be irreversible.
This is precisely called the pure right practice of skillful means.
Right practice possesses two capacities:
first, exiting from evil and entering into goodness.
Second, it emerges from the conditioned and enters the unconditioned;
therefore, this correct practice is the cause for abiding in the middle way.
Because it results in the purity of the fruit, the name "supramundane fruit" is established.
Purity of the fruit refers to *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
it is called purity of the fruit because all afflictions and burdens have been completely exhausted.
There are four defects associated with the outflows (*āsrava*).
These are impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The unconditioned possesses four virtues:
namely, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Because it is free from faults, it is called a supramundane fruit.
This means that by relying on the authentic teaching, contemplating correct principles,
and engaging in right practice, one attains the fruit of an Arya.
If the teaching contains error and does not manifest correct principle,
then all conduct undertaken in reliance upon it will be inverted.
Since such conduct is inverted, one will consequently obtain evil results.
Therefore, these four names are established for the sake of attaining these four kinds of purity.
Furthermore, they are intended so that, by relying on the authentic teaching, one may generate the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*),
and by relying on correct reasoning, one may give rise to the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).
By relying on correct practice, one attains the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Once these three types of wisdom are perfected, one shall attain the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*).

The four names are established because it is illogical for the perfuming of hearing and so forth to produce no fruit; these three are established based on both persons and dharmas.
